title: Configuring Action Inputs
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of configuring action inputs and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to configuring action inputs.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

items.title: Input formatting
items.text: Use `${{ ... }}` for workflow expressions and the correct context for the field. Treat event-derived values as data: pass untrusted text through an environment variable and quote it instead of inserting it into shell source.

content_blocks.code:
name: Set up Node.js
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
content_blocks.expected_output: The job selects Node.js 22, configures npm dependency caching, then installs versions recorded by the lockfile.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run only in a repository with a `package-lock.json`; compare the output of `node --version` and `npm ci`.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Update the runtime and lockfile together when migrating versions; check current action/runtime support before production use.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to configuring action inputs. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain configuring action inputs, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Decide when to run a shell command, invoke an action, or move logic into a repository script.

task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: The `with` mapping supplies documented action inputs; required inputs, expected data types, defaults, and expression values should match that action’s metadata.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: The `with` mapping supplies documented action inputs; required inputs, expected data types, defaults, and expression values should match that action’s metadata. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: The `with` mapping supplies documented action inputs; required inputs, expected data types, defaults, and expression values should match that action’s metadata.
`run` executes shell commands while `uses` invokes an action. Keep steps small, name them clearly, validate inputs, and review third-party action code and permissions.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
